taxonomic_note: Legacy Master Plant Pool name Tridens eragrostoides normalized to current accepted Triplasiella eragrostoides.
look_here_first: LOVEGRASS TRIDENS (Triplasiella eragrostoides; old Tridens/Triodia names): two REAL source-labelled mature open-panicle pictures help recognition, but purpletop, Texas tridens and purple lovegrass also have spreading heads. In the SECOND photo, the stiff bristly RIGHT-BACKGROUND grass is NOT this species. Confirm one mature true 3-veined lemma (~2–3 mm) with ONLY midnerve prolonged as a short mucro (not three long awns) plus inner membranous lacerate 1–3-mm ligule, and actual rooted plant. Research clue: Hagenbuch & Lemke 2015 list a Hays County Tharp s.n. TEX-LL voucher under Tridens eragrostoides; ORIGINAL specimen has not been inspected, county hold remains PROVISIONAL.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Hays-local source; Kew accepts Triplasiella eragrostoides and explicitly lists Tridens eragrostoides as a synonym.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: Installed for active visual learning; exact target-zone county reconciliation deferred.

morphology_keys.family_pattern: Poaceae: use growth habit, ligule, panicle architecture, spikelet form, lemma hairs and awns. For this old Tridens complex, panicle openness/color and current genus placement are especially useful.
best_field_traits: Open, spreading fine-branched panicle with small scattered spikelets. Purpletop/Texas tridens/lovegrasses ALSO have open heads, so this is a first clue only.

Tufted perennial; ACTUAL rooted base is not pictured. Texas Hill Country field treatment (2015) reports rhizomes and stolons ABSENT for Tridens eragrostoides, whereas the broader Flora Neomexicana Triplasiella generic diagnosis describes knotty rhizomatous bases. Distinguish true horizontal node-bearing rhizomes from a merely hard knotty crown on one documented living specimen; do not assert either with certainty from current head-only photographs.

Mature 3-veined lemma roughly 2–3.5 mm; central midnerve may extend as SHORT point/mucro, lateral veins do NOT form three equally projecting prongs in regional key. No current photograph resolves the veins.

ACTUAL true INNER blade/sheath is a 1–3 mm membranous ligule with a lacerate margin according to the Texas Hill Country vegetative treatment for Tridens eragrostoides. Generic Flora Neomexicana also discusses a ciliate membrane; do not conflate lacerate edges with a hair-only ligule or claim either appearance has been photographed for this source individual.

Open panicle with arching to spreading/drooping branches, broadly 10–30 cm long by 8–20 cm wide in taxonomic treatment; these values are reference context, NOT a size measured in current source photos.
morphology_keys.comparison_training: The airy lovegrass-like seedhead is the main cue. It is much more open than white tridens and now belongs in Triplasiella.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: FIRST: one physically archived CC BY/CC0/CC BY-SA photo of T. eragrostoides measured mature 3-veined lemma with central point and glumes, showing true size and all floret boundaries.
SECOND: true 1–3 mm ragged MEMBRANOUS ligule revealed at actual blade/sheath inner surface with a 1-mm ruler and precise arrow.

THIRD: a source-identified intact flowering plant with its actual fibrous-root crown exposed and centimeter ruler; check for a knotty crown and independently demonstrate whether horizontal, node-bearing rhizomes or stolons are REALLY PRESENT. Hagenbuch & Lemke (2015) report absence in Texas Hill Country material; Flora Neomexicana generic treatment describes knotty rhizomatous bases. Do not infer presence without same-voucher structural evidence.
FOURTH: matched macro comparison with native Tridens flavus and T. texanus mature lemma apex, not just whole flowerheads.
FIFTH: verify original photo-2 species voucher/GBIF photo-level license and ensure unrelated background grass is not mistaken for target.
crew_field_check: 1. Distinguish the foreground Triplasiella in photos 1–2 from unrelated BRISTLY grass at upper right in photo 2.
2. Compare photos 3–5: purpletop, Texas tridens and purple lovegrass are other native species with overlapping airy flowering heads. NEVER decide from one flowerhead silhouette.
3. Confirm a mature target spikelet and short 3-veined lemma under 10–20x beside a 1-mm ruler, glumes visible. No actual macro in current gallery.
4. Open actual blade/sheath and measure ragged membranous ligule. No actual macro in current gallery.
5. Preserve T. eragrostoides existing provisional Hays occurrence. This is not a finished county provenance audit.

comparisons.key_distinctions: TARGET Triplasiella eragrostoides — fairly broad open panicle, fine distant branches, darkening small spikelets; prior name Tridens eragrostoides. A midnerve that alone extends as a short projection is a useful fine distinction in Flora Neomexicana. NATIVE purpletop Tridens flavus — spreading/drooping OPEN panicle too, often purplish; beware previous overgeneralization that all Tridens are contracted. NATIVE Texas tridens Tridens texanus — arching open panicle, potentially quite similar from several feet away. Measure/inspect mature spikelet and lemma instead of using panicle outline as sole key. NATIVE purple lovegrass Eragrostis spectabilis — airy colored panicle and tuft, often superficially similar; check florets/lemma architecture in a confirmed plant. Triplasiella vs sandgrass Triplasis: the 2016 taxonomic treatment reports MUCH broader target panicles and different palea keels, plus absence of upper-sheath cleistogamous spikelets; those features are not verified in current images.

modern_species_diagnosis.quote_less_paraphrase: In key for historical Tridens eragrostoides, lemmas ca. 2–3 mm with only midnerve extended as a short point vs larger purpletop and mid+side nerves projecting.

crew_closeup_priority_20261023.first_clue: Follow a real flowering stem to the fully open, thin, somewhat drooping panicle, then isolate one mature floret. Open branching by itself does NOT separate lovegrass tridens from native purpletop, Texas tridens, or purple lovegrass.
crew_closeup_priority_20261023.highest_value_photo: Source-verified adult fertile lemma placed dorsal-face up beside 1 mm scale at 10–20×, capturing all three veins and whether ONLY the middle vein projects beyond its apex as a tiny mucro. Compare true purpletop mature floret at same magnification; New Mexico field key gives 2–3 mm lemma with only midnerve projecting in lovegrass tridens versus 4–4.5 mm with mid and lateral veins extending in purpletop.
crew_closeup_priority_20261023.second_photo: Open leaf blade–sheath junction with true ragged membranous ligule physically visible, ruler and attached shoot; do not claim current panicle photos prove it.
crew_closeup_priority_20261023.third_photo: Vouchered full perennial culm attached to base, crown and any rhizomes, with centimeter ruler. Current two source-labelled photos do not provide same-voucher rooting anatomy.
crew_closeup_priority_20261023.current_image_inventory: Two target-species JPEGs already local in GitHub, three local other-species comparison JPEGs in visual gallery. All five are local paths; no newly downloaded picture or remote hotlink introduced by this pass.
crew_closeup_priority_20261023.rights_policy: No unlicensed photo added. Never substitute a historic illustration for genuine macro photography; preserve all photo attribution and taxon-hold decisions.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 01 · OPEN HEAD
field_id_short_tiles.short: Tiny green or reddish spikelets on a very open, delicate panicle; not species-confirming alone
field_id_short_tiles.details: Start with real source-verified Triplasiella panicles in panels 0–1, fresh Texas flowering heads in panel 5, mature reddish spikelets in panel 6 and pale fresh branching spikelets in panel 11. Panels 8–9 show the plant among other low vegetation, but the underground rootstock is obscured and neighbors may be different grasses. The stiff bristly head BEHIND panel 1 belongs to another grass; its warning arrow must remain. Open branches are a first clue, not a confirmed ID: verify the tiny mature lemma and true collar under magnification.
field_id_short_tiles.status: REAL GREEN/DARK PANICLES AND FIELD HABIT NOW PHOTOGRAPHED — TINY LEMMA NOT YET CERTIFIED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · CHECK NATIVES
field_id_short_tiles.short: Purpletop and Texas tridens are also open!
field_id_short_tiles.details: Native LOOK-ALIKE photos in panels 2, 3, 4 respectively belong to purpletop (Tridens flavus), Texas tridens (Tridens texanus) and purple lovegrass (Eragrostis spectabilis). Purpletop can have an airy broadly spreading/drooping panicle TOO. Their glumes and mature lemma sizes must be examined as independent different-species specimens. Do not treat any image of them as a photograph of Triplasiella's true lemma or collar.
field_id_short_tiles.status: THREE NATIVE LOOK-ALIKE PANELS RETAINED — THEIR ORGANS DO NOT COUNT AS TRIPLASIELLA

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · MICROSCOPE LEMMA
field_id_short_tiles.short: Tiny green bract close-up now visible; only a dissected measured 3-veined lemma can confirm species
field_id_short_tiles.details: New CC0 panel 10 shows a REAL isolated-looking pale green flowering bract in close focus and panel 11 shows multiple attached green spikelets. HOWEVER the tiny bract has NOT been independently identified as lower glume, upper glume, lemma or palea, so DO NOT label it a 3-veined lemma. The published target diagnostic is a roughly 2–3-mm three-veined lemma with only its central midnerve protruding as a short point. Needed: a mature source-vouchered floret split apart dorsal side up, 1-mm ruler, actual veins and central mucro continuously visible. The historic 1900 illustration is NOT a photo.
field_id_short_tiles.status: REAL INDIVIDUAL GREEN FLORAL BRACT PHOTOGRAPHED — LEMMA ID/3 VEINS/MM MUCRO HOLD

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · TRUE COLLAR
field_id_short_tiles.short: Real outer leaf–sheath junction and culm node present; true inner 1–3 mm free ligule still missing
field_id_short_tiles.details: Panels 7 and 12 now show ACTUAL exact-species green external sheath, blade junction and a culm node. Panel 12 demonstrates why the pale STEM NODE is not the ligule; the diagnostic free inner membrane is located at the INSIDE blade–sheath junction. The 2015 Texas Hill Country treatment reports a 1–3-mm membranous ligule with lacerate margin; broader sources describe a ciliate membrane. Neither photo opens its free edge face-on with a true 1-mm scale. Obtain a single source-vouchered collar macro before adding ligule arrows or settling that source disagreement.
field_id_short_tiles.status: TRUE EXTERIOR COLLAR/NODE PHOTOS AVAILABLE — OPEN INNER LIGULE/MILLIMETER SCALE STILL MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · ROOTED PERENNIAL
field_id_short_tiles.short: Living basal shoot and habitat photographed; connected underground perennial crown remains unseen
field_id_short_tiles.details: Source-identified plants growing on Texas soil appear in panels 8–9; panel 7/12 show exterior lower shoot and leaf insertion. They establish live growth context, NOT a connected pulled-up perennial root crown. The 2015 Hill Country vegetative key reports a cespitose plant without stolons or rhizomes, while broader descriptions mention a knotty rhizomatous base; neither claim can be proven or resolved from these photos. Need an entire source-vouchered plant continuously showing flowering shoot, basal shoots, exposed attached roots and any underground lateral stems (IF PRESENT), preferably with a centimeter ruler. Do not identify mixed surrounding grasses as part of the focal plant.
field_id_short_tiles.status: REAL IN-GROUND FIELD HABIT, OUTER SHEATH AVAILABLE — EXPOSED ROOTED CROWN MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · MATURE FLORET SPLIT
field_id_short_tiles.short: Mature spikelets and a small real bract now photographed; dissected 3-veined lemma still required
field_id_short_tiles.details: Panels 6, 10 and 11 now give REAL near-view spikelets and one photographed individual green bract. The bract's identity is UNDETERMINED: we still need a mature specimen with physically separated lower and upper glumes, lemma and palea, each against a genuine 1-mm scale, so we can see 3 dorsal lemma veins and whether ONLY the central midnerve projects as a short mucro. Compare at identical scale to native purpletop rather than mistaking an awned look-alike for Triplasiella. The true free 1–3-mm ligule and extracted connected root crown are also open holds. New macro panels deliberately have zero speculative anatomy arrows.
field_id_short_tiles.status: FINE ANATOMY HOLD — BRACT VIEW REAL, LEMMA/GLUME PROOF + INNER LIGULE/ROOTS STILL REQUIRED

lane5_triplasiella_photo_finish_20261026.verified_observations: First target photo open thin branching flowering panicle. Second target foreground reddish spikelets and very obvious DIFFERENT bristly grass head in upper right; added only a negative-evidence arrow (target x71/y15), not guessed that other taxon. Roots, blade–sheath inner junction and photographed organ-scale lemmas absent.
lane5_triplasiella_photo_finish_20261026.scientific_difference: Texas Hill Country 2015 description (printed p.66) says no rhizomes/stolons for Tridens eragrostoides and 1–3-mm membranous ligule with lacerate margins; wider Flora Neomexicana genus account mentions knotty rhizomatous bases and ciliate ligule. Keep actual anatomy unresolved until one authenticated plant is photographed. A tuft is not independently proof of rhizomes or their absence.
